title: Rujuta Diwekar's Lauki Paneer Tikki Offers a Clever Fix for Fussy Young Eaters
excerpt: The celebrity nutritionist's bottle gourd and paneer tikki recipe transforms one of India's most shunned vegetables into a crispy, protein-rich snack that children actually want to eat.
body:
• Fitness expert Rujuta Diwekar has shared a bottle gourd (lauki) and paneer tikki recipe designed to help parents sneak this nutrient-dense vegetable into children's diets
  • Bottle gourd is approximately 96% water and contains just 14–15 calories per 100 grams, making it one of the lightest yet most hydrating summer vegetables
  • The recipe combines grated lauki with crumbled paneer, besan, and spices to create crispy, shallow-fried patties that mask the vegetable's mild flavour
  • For diaspora families, tikki-style preparations offer a practical bridge between heritage nutrition and children's taste preferences

The Lauki Problem Every Indian Parent Knows

Few vegetables in the Indian culinary canon inspire as much resistance from children as lauki—the pale, mild-tasting bottle gourd that grandmothers swear by and kids push to the edge of their plates. Celebrity nutritionist and bestselling author Rujuta Diwekar has addressed this perennial parenting challenge head-on, sharing a lauki and paneer tikki recipe that transforms the humble gourd into a crispy, golden snack, according to a report in The Indian Express.

Diwekar, who has built a following of over five million across social media through her advocacy of traditional Indian foods, has long championed seasonal, local vegetables over imported superfoods. Her lauki paneer tikki recipe is the latest demonstration that indigenous ingredients can be made appealing to even the most determined young holdouts.

What Makes the Recipe Work

The tikki format is central to the recipe's appeal. By grating the bottle gourd, squeezing out its considerable water content, and combining it with crumbled paneer, the vegetable's characteristically soft, watery texture is replaced with a firm, bindable mixture that can be shaped into patties.

"The tikki format offers a middle path—recognisable as a familiar "cutlet" or "patty" while delivering the nutritional benefits of a traditional Indian vegetable."

The base of grated lauki and paneer is bound with besan (gram flour) and seasoned with cumin, red chilli powder, garam masala, and fresh coriander. The tikkis are then shallow-fried until golden brown. The result is a snack with a crispy exterior and a soft, flavourful interior where the bottle gourd is virtually undetectable.

Variations documented across Indian cooking platforms such as Cookpad and Plattershare include additions like rice flour for extra crispiness, ajwain (carom seeds) for digestive benefits, and grated potato for binding.

A Nutritional Powerhouse in Disguise

Bottle gourd's reputation as a health food is well-earned. According to nutritional data compiled by health platforms Practo and DiabeSmart, 100 grams of lauki contains just 14–15 calories, 3.39 grams of carbohydrates, and 0.62 grams of protein, while being composed of approximately 96% water. It provides vitamin C (10.1 mg per 100g), potassium (150 mg), calcium (26 mg), and B-complex vitamins.

The vegetable's high water content makes it particularly valuable during Indian summers, when dehydration is a concern for active children. Ayurvedic practitioners have recommended lauki for centuries as a cooling food that reduces body heat—a property known in traditional medicine as pacifying "pitta."

Dietitian Rashmi Singh of Fitverse has noted that bottle gourd "helps keep the body hydrated and cool, particularly in hot climates," while also supporting digestive health through its soluble and insoluble fibre content.

Why the Tikki Format Matters

Diwekar's choice of the tikki as the delivery vehicle is deliberate. Nutritionists have observed that children's food resistance is often textural rather than flavour-based. The soft, watery consistency of standard lauki preparations like sabzi is precisely what many children reject.

By converting the vegetable into a crispy, hand-held format, the recipe leverages what food psychologists call the "snack effect"—children are far more likely to consume vegetables presented as finger foods than as components of a traditional thali. The addition of paneer, which provides approximately 18–20 grams of protein per 100 grams, elevates the nutritional profile well beyond what the vegetable alone delivers.

A Practical Option for Diaspora Kitchens

For Indian families abroad, the recipe addresses a challenge that extends beyond picky eating. Diaspora parents often struggle to maintain traditional dietary practices while their children's palates are shaped by Western food environments. Bottle gourd is increasingly available at Indian grocery stores across North America, the United Kingdom, and the Middle East, but convincing children to eat lauki ki sabzi remains difficult.

The tikki format offers a middle path—recognisable as a familiar "cutlet" or "patty" while delivering the nutritional benefits of a traditional Indian vegetable. The tikkis can also be batch-prepared and frozen, making them a convenient weeknight option or lunchbox addition.

Whether the lauki paneer tikki will convert every determined lauki-hater remains to be seen. But for parents who have exhausted the standard repertoire of hiding vegetables in parathas and mixing them into dal, it offers one more tool in an ancient and ongoing negotiation.
nri_angle: The tikki format bridges traditional Indian nutrition with Western snack culture, helping diaspora parents introduce bottle gourd to children raised in Western food environments.
